title: Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
raw_text: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services , including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors. The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials. “We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext,” Jeremiah Jasmin, security researcher at Microsoft, said in a blog post . Outages in cloud services bring about uncertainty and panic, an area where attackers always thrive, said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. “In cases where employees cannot access their emails and other applications, they will easily fall victim to any email promising to restore their service or help recover their account. This is especially dangerous for industries like finance, health care, government and educational institutions because employees in such organizations work with sensitive data and rely heavily on cloud services,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. Carefully constructed phishing trap The attackers used several techniques to make the emails appear relevant to recipients while evading basic email security filters. These included using specific sender domains, randomised outage-related subject lines, recipient-specific tracking links and a common non-Microsoft destination domain. The combination made the messages harder to identify through conventional pattern matching. The campaign began with emails sent from domains including moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Their subject lines followed the pattern “Outage” followed by a randomised string of characters. Microsoft also found a fake email conversation embedded in the message body, positioned to remain hidden from recipients. This appeared to be an attempt to evade email filtering mechanisms. The messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service health notifications. They used recipient-specific display name prefixes and referenced Microsoft services, including Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot. To create a sense of urgency, the emails claimed that messages held during the November 12 Exchange Online disruption would be deleted within 24 hours. Recipients were prompted to click a prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” button. The links contained recipient-specific tracking URLs that recorded or routed clicks before redirecting users to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html. One of the emails analysed by Microsoft had a subject line following the pattern “Outage – ” and a display name comprising a three-character organisation-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification.” Its body referred to a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12, claimed that four messages had been held during the outage and warned that they would be deleted within 24 hours unless restored. A successful credential theft attempt could expose more than an employee’s email account. Dhar explained that, depending on the permissions of the user, threat actors can gain access to sensitive emails, customer information, balance sheets, SharePoint, OneDrive Storage, and Microsoft Teams communication. Moreover, attackers can pretend to be representatives of the company and send believable emails to colleagues, clients, and contractors for the purposes of money fraud or theft of credentials. From containment to preparedness Microsoft said it had not observed any evidence of account compromise linked to the campaign. Messages detected and protected by Microsoft Defender for Office 365 were being blocked or quarantined. However, the company has advised organisations to remain vigilant and take several precautionary steps. CISOs should search email telemetry for the identified sender domains, display-name and subject-line patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domains. Matching messages should be quarantined, and copies already delivered to inboxes should be removed in accordance with the organisation’s incident response procedures. Security teams should also identify users who clicked on campaign links and review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to establish whether they reached the malicious destination and potentially entered their credentials. If credentials were exposed, organisations should immediately reset the affected passwords, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. They should also check affected accounts for suspicious sign-ins, unauthorised OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive or Teams. Microsoft has also advised security teams to block or closely monitor reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Employees should be reminded that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct users to non-Microsoft domains to recover held emails. Dhar added that organizations should make cybersecurity an integral part of their business continuity planning. Any technology disruption should trigger heightened security monitoring and clear internal communication to ensure employees know how to verify service-related updates. He also recommended conducting phishing simulations during such disruptions to test how employees respond to suspicious communications. CIOs and CISOs should regularly conduct tabletop exercises to assess their preparedness for attacks that exploit technology outages. The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld .

title: Google spots the first hacker AI system that finds and exploits flaws autonomously
raw_text: Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first time its researchers had observed such a system being used by threat actors. The findings, published in a report by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, suggest that attackers are moving beyond using generative AI to assist individual tasks and are beginning to automate larger portions of cyberattacks . The system could give attackers a way to exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities , known as n-days, before companies finish applying security updates. Google’s researchers discovered it on an exposed staging server and identified it as a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent. The framework connects to multiple large language models (LLMs) and is configured to examine changes in application code following security patches, identify vulnerabilities, and generate exploits without requiring an operator to direct each step. It can also execute the exploits automatically. Google found data exfiltrated from targeted victims on the server, along with scripts designed to support further activity after an initial compromise. Evidence suggested that the operator was particularly interested in French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries and the education sector. The report did not establish whether the framework’s autonomous operations were responsible for the theft. Google also cited a separate campaign involving vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers. According to research by GreyNoise referenced in Google’s report, a threat actor likely used AI tools to develop and test exploits before launching a campaign against hundreds of organizations four days after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. In separate cases, Google observed other AI frameworks being used by attackers. CAIRN was deployed in intrusion activity targeting organizations that included the US aerospace sector, while a customized platform based on PentAGI was used to conduct reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations across Asia. Pressure on enterprise response times Despite the growing use of AI in cyberattacks, the underlying techniques remain largely unchanged, according to Jonathan Ong , senior analyst at Omdia. “This is more of an acceleration of existing attack techniques,” Ong said. “These are pentesting/red-teaming frameworks with established techniques, albeit significantly sped up with an LLM model.” Keith Prabhu , CEO of Confidis, said there is still limited evidence that AI makes individual attacks more successful. The greater risk, he said, is that attackers could launch more attempts in less time, potentially increasing the number of successful compromises even if each attempt is no more effective. Ong said the frameworks typically generate considerable detectable activity, meaning enterprises with properly configured and monitored endpoint detection and response (EDR), extended detection and response (XDR), or managed detection and response (MDR) capabilities should still be able to identify much of the malicious activity. Google also warned that although the frameworks generate activity that makes detection easier, they remain capable of achieving their objectives. Rather than overhauling their defenses, security leaders should continue prioritizing established security practices, particularly cloud and identity hardening. Ong pointed to multifactor authentication, strong passwords, and measures to block repeated login attempts as effective safeguards. “The one thing that has changed is that the containment and response timeline needs to be faster, to match the speed at which attackers using these frameworks are moving,” Ong said. Prabhu said the problem is compounded by fragmented security visibility and response processes that still depend on manual decisions. He recommended that CISOs prioritize continuous asset discovery and risk-based vulnerability remediation. He also called for better detection capabilities that connect suspicious activity across enterprise environments. Amit Kumar Jena , development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations must give particular attention to vulnerabilities in systems exposed to the internet, where attackers could exploit flaws soon after they become public. “Internet-facing systems should be treated as their own class, with a fast-track patch path and virtual patching while fixes are tested,” Jena said. For incident containment, Prabhu suggested automating actions that are well understood and can be reversed, while retaining human approval for decisions that could have significant operational consequences. Jena also recommended defining in advance which containment actions could be automated, citing endpoint isolation and session revocation as examples. “The aim is not to remove human oversight, but to eliminate avoidable delays and regularly test that response works at the pace of an attack,” Prabhu said. Lower barriers for cybercriminals Open-source agentic frameworks could lower the technical barriers for less-experienced cybercriminals by helping them coordinate existing tools and adapt their attacks based on results, Prabhu said. However, these capabilities do not eliminate the need for technical expertise or guarantee successful compromises. Prabhu said smaller organizations and service providers with limited security resources could be particularly exposed. The risk is not necessarily concentrated in any particular industry, he added. Organizations with poorly maintained legacy systems or weak identity controls could face greater exposure regardless of their sector.
summary: Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first time its researchers had observed such a system being used by threat actors. The findings, published in a report by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, suggest that attackers are moving beyond using generative AI to assist individual tasks and are beginning to automate larger portions of cyberattacks . The system could give attackers a way to exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities , known as n-days, before companies finish applying security updates. Google’s researchers discovered it on an exposed staging server and identified it as a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent.

title: Alibaba touts 62% lower task costs with Qwen4-Max, adds cyber safeguards
raw_text: Alibaba has released Qwen4-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter flagship model, claiming it reduces the average cost of completing professional tasks by 62% compared with its predecessor while introducing additional safeguards against offensive cybersecurity capabilities and other high-risk uses. “According to Work360 — a proprietary benchmark evaluating performance on challenging industry tasks across 721 specialized fields — Qwen4-Max outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, overall while using 35% fewer tokens at High effort reasoning mode and reducing the average cost per task by around 60%,” Alibaba said in a blog post. The Qwen team’s announcement puts the average task cost at $1.67 for Qwen4-Max, compared with $4.43 for Qwen3.8-Max, representing a 62% reduction. The model keeps the 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone of its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, but activates about 71 billion parameters per token instead of about 95 billion, the company said. It supports a 1-million-token context window. The company attributed the savings to lower token use and new list prices of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, down from $2 and $6. Anthropic lists Claude Opus 5.5 at $20 per million output tokens. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said enterprises should treat the figure as a vendor benchmark rather than an assured reduction in their own AI spending. The relevant measure, he said, is the cost of an accepted result, including retries, reasoning tokens, and employee time spent checking outputs. “Alibaba has published the mileage it got on its own road, and a buyer’s bill depends on the road the buyer drives,” Gogia said. Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should measure successful task completion rather than token prices alone. “An enterprise should benchmark what it costs to complete 1,000 real business tasks successfully, not what it costs to generate a million tokens,” Kadakia said. Alibaba also cited improvements across coding and agentic evaluations, including Code Arena and Agents’ Last Exam. In an automotive manufacturing demonstration, the company said Qwen4-Max reduced manual workpiece programming time from approximately 475 minutes to 24 minutes. Security claims need independent testing Alongside the cost figures, Alibaba set out changes to what the model learns about hacking at the training-data stage. “For cybersecurity, we filter data according to the specific purpose of each task, retaining data for defensive tasks such as vulnerability verification, detection, and remediation, while removing data for offensive tasks aimed at enhancing attack capabilities,” the Alibaba blog post said. The company said code security checks added during training lifted the share of functions passing both functionality and security tests on Last Secure Code Bench from 22% to 31.8%. Its internal security experts found the model’s defensive capabilities had “improved substantially,” the post added. Kadakia questioned whether offensive and defensive cybersecurity knowledge can be reliably separated through training-data filtering. “One of the fundamental challenges with cybersecurity AI is that offensive and defensive knowledge are largely the same knowledge,” he said, noting that understanding SQL injection is necessary both to exploit and prevent it. Gogia said the distinction requires independent validation, recommending that CISOs seek assessments from government evaluators or established external red teams rather than rely solely on Alibaba’s internal testing. The announcement follows an October investigation by Canadian AI company Cohere, which reported that an earlier Alibaba model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, attempted to send a test file to an Alibaba Cloud storage destination in Beijing during a security test. Cohere said its sandbox blocked the request. A subsequent investigation by Check Point replayed the behaviour 64 times and found 52 different destination hosts. It suggested unpredictable model behaviour was a more likely explanation than a deliberately configured backdoor. The incident involved an experimental model, not Qwen4-Max. Besides, Government evaluators have begun testing Chinese models independently. In July, the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation found that the safeguards on Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 allowed assistance with agentic cyber exploit development. Gogia said CISOs should treat Alibaba’s filter “as a promise until a government evaluator or an established outside red team has tested it.” Data governance and open-weight risks For enterprises outside China, Gogia said the geographic scope of Alibaba’s global service, prompt-retention policies, and jurisdiction governing stored data should be considered before deploying the model for sensitive workloads. He pointed to prompt retention of up to 30 days and longer retention of flagged content, including under zero-retention arrangements. Kadakia said enterprises should examine where prompts, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and logs are processed, who can access them, and what permissions agents have across internal systems. “The biggest risk with enterprise AI is no longer simply what information employees type into a chatbot. It is what an autonomous agent can access, what decisions it can make, and what actions it can execute across connected enterprise systems,” he said. Alibaba also plans to release smaller Qwen4 models with open weights. Kadakia said developers modifying those models through fine-tuning should not assume the original security safeguards will remain intact. “Safety training is not a permanent property of a model,” he said, recommending fresh adversarial testing and controls over tool access for customised versions. Gogia similarly recommended reassessing each modified model rather than automatically inheriting the original model’s security assurances. The article originally appeared on InfoWorld .

The Qwen team’s announcement puts the average task cost at $1.67 for Qwen4-Max, compared with $4.43 for Qwen3.8-Max, representing a 62% reduction. The model keeps the 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone of its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, but activates about 71 billion parameters per token instead of about 95 billion, the company said.

title: The benign true positive: When trusted AI agents look like attackers
raw_text: A coding agent opens hundreds of files, launches command-line tools and connects to an internal service to complete a task. A support agent authenticates to several systems, retrieves customer records and updates another application. A workflow agent enumerates cloud resources in seconds, then moves to the next stage of its assignment. To an endpoint, identity, or cloud security platform, these sequences can resemble reconnaissance, credential access, lateral movement, or the early stages of exfiltration. The control is accurately identifying behavior associated with an attack, and the agent is carrying out an approved business task. I am beginning to see this pattern as enterprises deploy AI agents across software development, customer support, finance, IT and security. I call it the benign true positive: an accurate detection of attack-like behavior generated by legitimate machine activity. For CISOs, this exposes a foundational assumption beneath behavioral security . For decades, attack-like behavior justified immediate suspicion because legitimate systems rarely operated with the speed, breadth and autonomy now common among AI agents. That assumption is weakening, and security leaders need to prepare their teams, processes and technology portfolios for the consequences. Behavioral baselines were built around people Modern detection systems rely heavily on patterns associated with expected human activity. People read files at a human pace, move between applications in recognizable sequences, and generally interact with systems one action at a time. An account that suddenly enumerates thousands of resources or launches a chain of processes across several environments deserves investigation. AI agents follow a different operating pattern. They gather context broadly, perform tasks in parallel and move across systems according to the needs of an assigned objective. A coding agent may inspect an entire repository before changing a few lines. A support agent may authenticate to several applications because resolving a customer request requires data from each one. The resulting telemetry frequently matches the signals security tools were designed to detect. Existing controls will keep generating alerts, and those alerts will often be technically correct. Security teams must determine whether the behavior reflects an authorized task, a compromised agent, manipulated instructions, stolen credentials, or an attacker imitating normal agent activity. A broad suppression rule may reduce noise but also create a blind spot. Attackers will naturally look for trusted agent identities, approved workflows and familiar machine-speed patterns that help them blend into the environment. Intent becomes the missing layer Security tools observe actions such as process launches, file reads, authentication events, API calls, or network connections. Intent sits in the surrounding context. Investigators need to know who owns the agent, what task it was assigned, who initiated the task, which systems it was authorized to use, what data it could access and whether its actions stayed within approved boundaries. They also need to determine whether another user, process, or external input altered the agent’s instructions. Those answers may be distributed across identity systems, agent orchestration platforms, cloud infrastructure, business applications, ticketing systems and the security stack. Reconstructing the event requires correlation across these sources and a clear account of what the agent was trying to accomplish. A large enterprise may soon operate thousands of agents across business and technical functions. Human analysts cannot manually reconstruct every event at that scale. Security operations will need investigative capacity that can recover intent at machine speed and present conclusions grounded in observable evidence. 3 investment priorities for CISOs 1. Agent identity and governance The first priority is agent identity and governance . Every agent should have a clear owner, a defined purpose, credentials scoped to its responsibilities and documented access to applications, tools and data. The SOC should be able to connect each action to the workflow, user request, or business process that initiated it. This requires an inventory of active agents, lifecycle controls, access reviews, approval requirements for sensitive actions and audit trails that connect behavior to an accountable owner. Shared service accounts and broad permissions slow investigations and make containment harder. Purpose-specific identities and task provenance give the SOC the context needed to identify misuse. 2. Investigation architecture The second priority is investigation architecture. Security leaders should evaluate whether their current stack can assemble evidence across endpoint, identity, cloud, network, SaaS and agent platforms. A useful system should reconstruct the sequence of events, apply organizational context, document missing information and explain how it reached a conclusion. AI investments in the SOC should support evidence gathering, cross-system correlation, adaptive reasoning and clear escalation whenever the available data cannot support a confident determination. 3. Team design The third priority is team design. Analysts will increasingly govern systems that investigate both human and machine behavior. Their expertise will shape operating boundaries, exception handling, detection logic and the context used during investigations. Security leaders should invest in detection engineering, threat hunting, identity governance and agent oversight skills. Analysts need time and authority to examine recurring behavioral collisions, refine access policies, improve workflows and challenge automated conclusions. Each benign true positive can become a source of operational learning about how agents are being used and where controls need to mature. A new operating model for the SOC The traditional SOC sends alerts to analysts, who gather evidence and decide what happened. AI agents will add another source of high-volume activity, and many resulting alerts will be accurate detections of legitimate behavior. The SOC needs an operating model built around rapid interpretation. For an authorized event, the investigation should show that a specific agent accessed particular systems under an approved identity, pursued a valid task, remained within its permissions and produced no evidence of deviation. For a risky event, it should show where the activity exceeded the agent’s expected scope and why human review or containment is required. This level of clarity preserves sensitive detections, keeps analysts focused on cases that demand judgment, and creates a practical path for building trust in increasingly autonomous systems through visible evidence, explicit accountability and measurable outcomes. Preparing for the next source of alert volume CISOs should begin by mapping where agents already operate across the organization. Many will discover activity introduced through developer tools, SaaS platforms, departmental automation and enterprise applications with embedded agent capabilities. The next step is to connect agent ownership, identity, permissions, task provenance and policy to security operations. Teams should test how existing controls respond to representative agent workflows and track benign true positives as a distinct operational category. AI agents are changing the meaning of normal behavior. Security leaders who prepare now can preserve visibility, strengthen governance and build a SOC capable of understanding the purpose behind machine-speed activity. Trusted machines will increasingly look like attackers. The organizations that can recover intent quickly will be best positioned to tell the difference.

A support agent authenticates to several systems, retrieves customer records and updates another application. A workflow agent enumerates cloud resources in seconds, then moves to the next stage of its assignment. To an endpoint, identity, or cloud security platform, these sequences can resemble reconnaissance, credential access, lateral movement, or the early stages of exfiltration.

title: AI-written patches are becoming attack maps for hackers
raw_text: This summer, the maintainers of vm2, an open-source JavaScript sandboxing library with 1 million downloads per week, shipped fixes for 34 separate sandbox-escape vulnerabilities and Anthropic’s Claude co-wrote 19 of them. Weeks later, a security researcher pointed an AI agent at one of the advisories and asked for a way around the patch. The agent delivered. Shayaun Nejad, lead product security engineer at Rubrik, ran vulnerability variant analysis on the vm2 patch while preparing for a talk he held at the recent [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He wanted to highlight the challenges his development team faced when dealing with a flood of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and noted that the same bugs kept being rediscovered later in new testing runs despite being fixed by AI-assisted pipelines. “Sometimes the [vulnerability] variant wouldn’t be caught until the model variation got better or the model used chaining analysis at a higher degree once it improved in order to find those variants,” he said. “Sometimes it was in the exact same spot, sometimes it was something that was related, that was a neighbor, but variant analysis is basically something that has been popping up, and it’s a context magnet, too.” With the rate of published CVEs higher than ever due to AI assistance, software developers are actually disclosing the types of vulnerabilities their platforms are susceptible to, and the patches for these flaws can serve as blueprints for attackers, Nejad warned. Sometimes it’s as simple as pointing an AI agent at a codebase with its historical vulnerabilities as context and telling it to go hunt for variants, he said. Rubrik’s experience reflects a broader asymmetry that other researchers have observed in recent months: AI models have become very good at offense — finding vulnerabilities and building exploits — while their defensive skills, such as writing secure code and correct patches, have lagged behind . Also at the [un]prompted conference, OpenAI security researcher Tim de Waal showed how an AI agent patched two vulnerabilities in the firmware of a network access point. For one issue, the agent rebuilt the vulnerable function without the stack canaries the original code had, silently removing a defensive protection. For the other, the generated patch filtered out double-quote characters in the attacker input but missed that using single quotes would have bypassed the fix. Controlled studies found the same issue at scale. When researchers at 1Password’s Off-by-1 Labs used AI agents to repeatedly generate patches for the same six known vulnerabilities in complex open-source projects, about half of the 6,080 resulting patch candidates left at least one attack path open , with agents sometimes missing identical instances of the same bug in other parts of the code. More recently, in a benchmark test called P2Patch , researchers pitted two AI agents against each other: one wrote exploits for 101 real vulnerabilities, and the other patched the code until the exploits stopped working. Then the first agent attacked the patched programs again, looking for a different way to trigger the same flaw. In 41 of the 101 cases, it succeeded, sometimes multiple times for subsequent patches. Of course, human-written patches are not infallible either. Security firm Trail of Bits reviewed the fixes developers submitted for 2,265 vulnerabilities found during its consulting assessments over several years and one in eight failed to fully resolve the reported issues. In one case the company documented, a human maintainer and an AI agent working as part of the Patch the Planet initiative separately wrote patches for the same memory-safety bug in the freenginx web server, and both patches introduced the same crash during request cleanup. Organizations turn to AI patching because humans can’t keep up The issue is not that AI always writes worse patches than humans, although the failure rate of AI-written patches might be higher, but that the rate of vulnerability discovery is now so fast that humans alone can’t keep up. This is combined with the offensive capabilities of AI agents that enable attackers to analyze and reverse engineer patches at machine speed. Seven months after launching its Mythos-powered Glasswing vulnerability-hunting program , Anthropic’s public ledger counted 37,966 findings. Only 217 of the 7,349 flaws that were made public had been fixed, according to a recent analysis from vulnerability intelligence firm VulnCheck. Not all findings turn out to be security vulnerabilities, but Anthropic claims a true positive rate of 94.2%, which, given the small number of fixes, highlights the deluge of reports that maintainers have to triage and deal with. “Progress on software security used to be limited by how quickly we could find new vulnerabilities,” Anthropic wrote in its initial Glasswing update . “Now it’s limited by how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch the large numbers of vulnerabilities found by AI.” And this is not just a problem for open-source projects. After Bank of America let Anthropic’s models loose on its own systems, the bank added 1,000 outside contractors in the second quarter of this year to help with the patching work, on top of the roughly 3,000 existing staff. They were still on the job in October, CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC . By July, Meta was using AI to write fixes for 40% of its critical vulnerabilities, and almost half of those patches landed in production unchanged. Despite that, the exposure time did not go down, Meta software engineer David Molnar said in a separate presentation at [un]prompted. That’s because the AI-proposed patches still had to be reviewed by humans, while the amount of new code grew more than 100% year over year, with more than 80% of it attributed to AI coding agents. “Everyone is drowning in stuff to review,” Molnar said, adding that his team has worked with directors and product managers internally to find more places where automation can be introduced, including in the review process, shifting it from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop . “You can automate everything upstream of AI, and then just completely overwhelm your poor humans on the other end,” he said. “Which is why you have to take a look at the entire pipeline and automate all of it.” In June, the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams (FIRST) projected around 66,000 CVE assignments for this year. With two months left, the number is already approaching 100,000. Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday alone addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities compared to only 180 in October 2025. Closed-source patches are not safe from AI analysis If AI agents are scouring code repositories for vulnerability variants, one might be inclined to think that closed-source sofware, where the patch is usually inside a compiled binary, are safer. That’s not necessarily the case given that AI models are now also great at reverse engineering, and some people use them to create open-source replicas of complex proprietary products, for example Adobe Photoshop . In June, when Anthropic’s researchers tested what an attacker can do with AI-assisted patch diffing , they gave a model nothing beyond what’s public on patch day. It produced a working exploit within an hour of a Firefox fix landing. On Windows, given vulnerable and patched binaries plus decompilation output, the same approach built eight full privilege-escalation chains from 21 kernel vulnerabilities for roughly $2,000 each. “In some ways, N-days are the more dangerous of the two [compared to zero-days], because the patch itself provides a roadmap to the bug,” the Anthropic researchers said at the time. A team of researchers from Fudan University in Shanghai, China, built an LLM-assisted binary diffing framework and analyzed 76 recent patches from 62 closed-source applications across 25 vendors. According to their paper published this month, the framework flagged 63 of the patches as incomplete and manually confirmed 56, of which 26 could be bypassed into new vulnerabilities, resulting in 19 CVE assignments and $28,100 in bug bounties. Comparing a vulnerable build against a patched one to locate the changed code has been a standard practice for security researchers for years. The difference now is the speed and lack of skill needed thanks to AI. And even though the latest frontier AI models might have API guardrails that make reverse engineering or binary diffing harder, the open-weight models have become capable enough. Taesoo Kim, vice president of security research at Microsoft, also warned during the [un]prompted conference that AI has drastically reduced the time needed for binary-diff analysis and exploit creation, and noted that Microsoft has to also be extremely careful when publishing CVEs and push updates quickly to customers. The more recent frontier models have started refusing such binary analysis work due to stricter guardrails, but a lot of people use open-weight models instead, such as Qwen, Kimi, and GLM, because “they are extremely capable,” he said. Exploiting the patch gap is now easy Last month, the Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are increasingly taking advantage of the time gap between when information about a potential vulnerability becomes available in a code commit or test release in one project and when the patch trickles down to other projects. Their report included examples of attackers exploiting security fixes revealed in Chromium builds, the open-source browser that serves as the base for Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and other browsers, before those fixes were integrated in those downstream browsers. “This is patch-gap abuse,” the Edge team said . “The technique is not new, but the speed and expertise required is changing. AI-assisted analysis and exploit development could compress work that once took weeks into hours, increasing the chance that a usable exploit emerges while either exposure window remains open.” Researchers from Epoch AI recently used GLM 5.3 to emulate an unsophisticated attacker and target the Firefox patch gap. Using about $1,000 in API credits and as little as 12 hours of work per target, it compromised every Firefox release shipped between Sept. 17 and Oct. 26. “We did not trigger any safeguards or refusals from any provider,” the researchers wrote . In response, the Mozilla team has decided to take several actions to prevent patch gap abuse, for example by no longer releasing the regression tests associated with security fixes. “We’ve observed that GLM 5.3 is much less effective at patch-gapping when a regression test is not present, so we’ve reintroduced a practice of keeping these confidential until after the fix has shipped,” Firefox CTO Bobby Holley wrote . More diligence in patching, not less disclosure In a report last month dubbed PatchSlop, security firm Terra found that the rate of incomplete or broken fixes across open-source projects increased eightfold this year . “A patch that only blocks the reported input can give the impression the bug is addressed even if it’s still there in the underlying code,” the company’s researchers said. “It functions as a map for attackers, marking out both vulnerable code and what the defender thought the bug was. Looking just outside the diff (another encoding, another address range, another path into the same function) is one of the cheapest forms of bug hunting. We believe a growing share of attacker effort, and AI tokens, goes into exactly this.” The answer is not for open-source projects and software companies to hide vulnerability details and stop publishing security advisories, but to produce better patches. And some researchers believe this is possible, even when patching gets automated with the help of AI agents. In Rubrik’s case, after the company noticed that bugs it had marked as fixed kept coming back, Nejad’s team added its own variant hunting step that runs automatically in the pipeline after fixes are developed. The company began routing simple bugs to AI patching while reserving complex flaws, such as authentication bypasses, for human engineers. “Yes, attackers do have that context, but you have that context first, and you can act on that,” Nejad said. In a blog post this month , OpenAI noted that its Linux vulnerability research and patching pipeline needed iterative testing and variant analysis because initial patches “failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.” “We recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more,” the company’s researchers said. The Open Source Security Foundation’s guidance for AI-assisted patching also advises teams to “have a new discovery agent probe the patch as an attacker” and Trail of Bits has released an agent skill that requires testing at least one distinct variant based on the bug’s root cause before a patch can be submitted. “It is clear there needs to be greater diligence and rigor when patching vulnerabilities,” Terra CEO Shahar Peled told CSO. “This means finding the root cause of any flaw, searching across the codebase for similar bugs and re-testing the system to ensure the patch itself doesn’t introduce a new vulnerability.”

title: Interview: Loïc Giraud, vice-president of data and AI foundation, Novo
raw_text:
After spending time at a startup, Loïc Giraud, vice-president of the data and artificial intelligence (AI) foundation at healthcare and pharmaceutical company Novo, returned to what he knows best just over two years ago – helping a blue-chip enterprise exploit its information assets.

Computer Weekly last spoke with Giraud in May 2022, when he was global head of digital platform and product delivery at Novartis, where he managed a data-led digital transformation programme across the healthcare specialist. After more than 11 years with Novartis, he spent 12 months in the startup sector as chief operating officer at AI technology specialist Calibo.

“When you’re running a startup in the early phase, you have to do a lot of sales and marketing, which is probably not my core competence,” he says, reflecting on the entrepreneurial experience. “I realised I wanted to go back to enterprise. I came to Novo to lead the data and AI function. I’ve been doing that since August 2024.”

Giraud describes his past two years at Novo as a rollercoaster. He’s had to make tough choices to help the organisation embrace emerging technologies. From data platforms to agentic services, his team has built the foundations to help the business grow. Looking back on the transformations they’ve enabled, Giraud recognises it’s been an interesting ride.

“They recruited me because they were not successful in bringing data and the AI function together,” he says. “That was my remit when I joined. I think we have a clear perspective on how we can become the most AI-driven healthcare company in the world, and how we drive patient acquisition and patient adherence, and treat their needs effectively.”

Providing capabilities

Giraud joined a team with decentralised activities that lacked clear focus on business priorities and strategic ambitions. While some teams did good work, he was eager to bring more structure to data operations.

“It took me a bit of time to understand how everything functioned,” he says. “We had to focus on explaining to stakeholders, trying to change the operating model and the incentives, and then we started to build trust by creating products that bring value while trying to develop capabilities that help you for the long term.”

Giraud says his team has made considerable progress since 2024. During this time, emerging technology has begun to play a bigger role in business operations. As more people across business functions have started exploring AI-enabled services, the emphasis has shifted.

“That’s a big paradigm shift in the industry,” he says. “There used to be a lot of central software engineers and AI engineers, and then technology became so simple that you’re now more or less becoming an orchestrator and enabler, and then you decentralise the execution.”

Today, Giraud describes his role at Novo as establishing AI and data strategy: “How do you align that with the business priorities across the respective business domains? How do you execute that through a portfolio of products, as well as building the right platform capability that helps you to scale?”

Giraud says orchestration and enablement involve establishing the platforms and processes that allow professionals to build their own solutions to business challenges. “You have to provide the capabilities in which they can be self-sufficient, and then the guardrails and controls,” he adds.

“And I would say 80% of our time is focused on that area. The remaining 20% is building complex solutions or helping the business identify problems that need solutions. We think about those problems to the point that a future product line can be established.”

Empowering and automating

Giraud says the general direction of the firm’s digital transformation is about creating data-enabled healthcare solutions for customers. His team’s efforts centre on three areas: empowerment, automation, and reinvention.

“With empowerment specifically, how do you provide the digital fluency for your end-users to be able to actually perform the work differently?” he says. “So, technically, training and the tools are required for them to be assisted and then to be more creative, and to spend less time on routine work and then be more focused on innovation.”

Emerging technology plays a crucial role in empowerment. Giraud says more than 60% of Novo employees now use AI every week. The data team has helped establish ChatGPT as the company’s conversational front-end user interface. They’re building connections so users can chat to data in key systems, such as the firm’s Snowflake data platform.

For automation, the data team considers how emerging technologies such as agentic AI can reimagine business process workflows.

“You can eliminate a lot of steps and use agents to perform many of these tasks, and sometimes you have to differentiate between what humans need to do versus what the agents need to do – and this is a core of our business,” says Giraud.

He adds that this reimagination is a work in progress. The business has identified where agents can automate certain workflows and is exploring how AI is used across key lines of business, including human resources and procurement processes. The company has almost 8,000 agents in production, including for productivity and research and development.

While the progress in automation is impressive, Giraud says he wouldn’t describe Novo as an agentic business: “No, I would not say we are at that stage yet. It will probably take another two years to get there. I must say that compared to last year, when we had none, I think we are quite far right now.”

Centralising data services

One key area of progress is the firm’s Snowflake data platform. The implementation pre-dated Giraud’s arrival, but he’s continued to hone the deployment since joining Novo, including working with the technology specialist to support agentic explorations.

“Snowflake has been established mostly in the commercial space,” he says. “All our affiliates use the same platform for their commercial activities, so it’s the only platform sales and marketing use. When I joined, the platform was decentralised. We had different Snowflake teams globally. We centralised that approach into one single function.”

The company’s corporate affiliates and subsidiaries across 80 countries use the platform for operational activities, including sales, marketing, finance, and procurement. Around 25,000 people in the affiliates use the platform directly or indirectly. With more than 900TB of data in Snowflake, Novo is using the scalable cloud-based platform to feed agentic systems.

“Every company must reinvent itself continually”

Loïc Giraud, Novo

Giraud says the company uses the personal productivity agent Snowflake CoWork to help professionals query data. Novo staff can use CoWork to ask questions in natural language and to access information that helps them position the right drugs to patients. The agent also helps the company to translate product information across its affiliates.

“It’s mostly around consumer understanding and portfolio management,” he says, referring to the use of the Snowflake platform and CoWork. “The technology provides the information to support the field force. The intent is to help our field reps prepare for their visits to the healthcare providers, whether they have a voice interaction or use a chat interface.”

Novo is also exploring CoCo, Snowflake’s coding agent that assists professionals with machine learning workflows. Giraud says data engineers are building new connections to services with the agent.

“They’re increasing the depth in the stack,” he says, reflecting on Snowflake’s recent product developments, which Computer Weekly saw first-hand in San Francisco. “They’ve completely revamped their strategy and how they position and drive the AI agenda.”

Reinventing the business

The final area of Novo’s digital transformation focuses on reinvention – and Giraud suggests this is a key component as the firm continues to grow. The business has grown by almost 20% annually during the past four years and aims to reach 60 million patients by 2030.

“Every company must reinvent itself continually,” he says, reflecting on the rapid pace of change in the AI age.

One key area of innovation is drug discovery. Novo’s US patent for semaglutide, the main ingredient in its Wegovy and Ozempic weight-loss drugs, is set to expire in 2032.

“We need to find the next generation of drugs,” he says. “Now, with frontier AI and access to IT infrastructure you never had before, you can do things much faster.”

Another key area of reinvention is consumerisation. Novo CEO Mike Doustdar said recently that the rapid growth of obesity treatments has transformed the firm’s patient base and shifted the market toward a more consumer-oriented model, where patients move on and off therapies more frequently than in traditional diabetes care.

Giraud recognises that his team can help Novo meet customers’ fast-changing requirements, including through product and service developments.

“We have an advanced digital innovation engine in research that helps us to identify a lot of potential targets that we are putting into execution,” he says, suggesting the engine is powered by frontier AI models.

“For consumerisation, we’ve launched our Novocare pharmacy service. It’s our front door for consumers to buy our products. We’ve also built a supporting data ecosystem in which we can better understand consumer needs and then activate that demand accordingly.”

Inside and outside the organisation, Giraud suggests the pace of change has never been quicker. He says the past two years have seen the most radical transformations witnessed during his 25-year career. However, this period of change is just the beginning. He expects significant disruption in the pharma industry during the next decade. Professionals must prepare for this continual transformation.

“What I can see right now is mind-blowing,” he says. “I’m more worried for the new generation of workers because they will have to be much more agile and adaptable than we have been. That’s probably my advice for any of these professionals – start to learn with AI and continue to be adaptable to change.”

title: Google widens sovereign cloud with Gemini, key and audit tools
raw_text:
Google has added Gemini models to Google Cloud Dedicated, its partner-operated sovereign cloud offering, to widen the choice of artificial intelligence (AI) available to organisations that need locally controlled infrastructure.

The company announced the change at its Sovereign AI Summit in Brussels this week, alongside a preview of confidential external key management (cEKM) and new audit frameworks that map regulation to enforced controls.

Sovereign cloud offerings from Google come in three forms:

  1. Google Cloud Data Boundary, which applies data residency, access and encryption controls on the public cloud;
  2. Google Cloud Dedicated, which is isolated infrastructure operated by an independent local partner;
  3. Google Distributed Cloud, which runs in a customer’s own datacentre, and can be connected or fully air-gapped.

Google introduced the three-tier portfolio in May 2025 and set out its underlying commitments in February 2026 to cover local investment, operational continuity, customer control of data and open technology. The Brussels announcements build on that base rather than replacing it.

Gemini already runs in Google Cloud under a commitment to process customer data in-region, and on Google Distributed Cloud. In France, S3NS has made managed model serving and inference generally available on PREMI3NS, its cloud built on Google Cloud Dedicated. Teams can deploy open models from Mistral and Google, or their own tuned models, inside an environment S3NS controls.

Confidential external key management, now in preview, lets customers or local partners hold root keys outside Google Cloud while key operations run inside a hardware-attested Confidential Computing environment. Google said the design keeps latency low and reliability high. A partnership with Telefónica, also in preview, adds Spain to the countries where organisations can hold keys locally, alongside France, Germany and Italy. Key custody is a common sticking point in regulated procurement, where buyers must show who controls encryption.

S3NS and the Thales German launch

Google’s European sovereign cloud rests on local operators. In France, S3NS – the Thales and Google Cloud joint venture – has achieved SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from ANSSI, the national cyber security agency, and now serves more than 130 customers. Thales is moving 80% of its own applications onto the platform.

Hélène Bringer, president of S3NS, said the venture’s proposition was “to have data sovereignty in our trusted cloud”. S3NS struck a flagship partnership with SAP in May, with SAP Rise set to become the second software-as-a-service (SaaS) solution on PREMI3NS next year.

The model is now moving into Germany. With Thales, Google Cloud Dedicated is in preview there, run from three datacentres in Berlin. Marcus Mühling, chief executive of Secure Cloud Germany, said the local operation had submitted its C3A documentation to the BSI, Germany’s federal cyber security agency, on 1 October and received positive feedback. It is working towards ISO 27001 and C5 certification by the end of the first quarter, with operations due in the second quarter.

“If your clients have to make extreme choices – either sovereignty or innovation – that’s broken,” Mühling said.

Meanwhile, Data Boundary frameworks aim to map local and regional regulatory requirements to enforced, auditable controls. A framework for Switzerland is available now, and Google plans one for the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act (Dora) for financial services next. Audit Manager then gives auditors continuous, machine-readable evidence. Google positioned the frameworks as a way to cut the engineering effort that sovereignty audits usually demand, which can be a persistent drag on regulated cloud projects.

Regulated workloads often stall because the security, identity and monitoring tools teams rely on are missing from a sovereign environment. Google said more than a dozen software suppliers, including European providers Memority and Tsuga, have now validated their products on Google Cloud Dedicated to close that gap.

It also launched the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI, an equity-free programme that gives startups in regulated sectors engineering support, mentorship and access to local cloud providers.

Marianne Janik, vice-president for EMEA North at Google Cloud, said the release removed a long-standing trade-off. “Organisations that need a locally operated cloud will no longer have to choose between frontier AI and control,” she said. “Alongside Gemini, we’re announcing four more ways to put control in your hands.”

Google frames sovereignty as a property of the whole stack. Janik argued that a stack is only as sovereign as its weakest layer – the layer a customer cannot control or replace – and that the answer is a composable stack with verifiable controls and exit options at every layer.

Google has pitched the portfolio on verifiable control. That answers critics who argue that hyperscaler sovereignty commitments rest on trust.

Its Cloud Dedicated offer lets customers block software updates in exceptional circumstances and keep operating for up to 12 months if their connection to Google is severed. This aims to answer the continuity concern that underpins the “kill switch” debate.

Google’s sovereign cloud push matters beyond the EU. UK organisations that run workloads in Europe face the same questions, and UK CIOs are watching how far the EU’s Cloud and AI Development Act (Cada) reaches as Brussels builds out its full-stack sovereignty package.

The practical test will be evidence of deployments. Buyers increasingly have to show regulators and auditors how data and keys are held, who can access them and what happens if a provider is cut off.

title: Fintech pioneer Anne Boden back with agentic AI-focused bank
raw_text:
Starling bank founder Anne Boden has revealed her next venture to be an agentic artificial intelligence (AI)-focused bank.

The bank, Lockwood, will initially attempt to gain an Electronic Money Institution (EMI) licence from the Financial Conduct Authority in 2027, before a full banking licence in 2028. It is targeting one million customers in its first year.

Boden, who left Starling in 2023, sold her shares in the firm, and is reported to be providing the new company’s initial funding.

She told The Sunday Times that the bank is “going to be built by agents, to serve customers that want to use agents, and then be defended by agents”.

On its website, Lockwood describes its approach to AI and its security. “You’re ready to welcome AI assistants into your life, with all the convenience and financial freedom they offer,” it says. “Yet, at the same time, more fraudsters are using AI to try to break into people’s accounts. Most banks will respond with more passwords, more checks and more tracking. Lockwood is different. Lockwood is building its current account with fewer ways in, and Lockwood guards every one of them.”

According to Lockwood, it is a current account that “lets your AI agent pay for things safely, within limits you set, for people and small businesses in the UK.”

“Ten years ago, we built digital banking around the smartphone,” she said. “Today, the interface of personal finance is shifting again – from apps that you tap to intelligent agents that act on your behalf. If an AI agent is going to shop for you, pay your bills or manage your money, your bank account needs to be engineered specifically to govern that relationship safely. Lockwood is about giving people the confidence to embrace agentic AI while keeping absolute control over their finances.”

Boden founded Starling in 2014, and it received its banking licence in 2016, launching the following year. In October 2020, it made its first monthly profit of £800,000, becoming the first UK digital challenger bank to do so, and it reached fintech unicorn status in 2021.

Read more about Boden: Banker’s startup experience feathers the nest for Starling Bank

Boden is an IT professional who got into banking. She gained a BSc in computer science and chemistry, and an MBA.

Boden joined Lloyds Bank in the early 1980s, when, as she told Computer Weekly in a 2015 interview, she was “doing fintech before fintech was fashionable”.

After Lloyds Bank, her career has included a period heading up UK IT at Standard Chartered; being one of the original designers of the Clearing House Automated Payments System; a role as a strategy and technology consultant at PWC; restructuring European operations at UBS; holding the global chief information officer job for reinsurance at Aon; and running business in 34 countries for ABN Amro, and subsequently RBS, when it took over the Dutch bank.

But it was after leaving RBS in 2011 – to spend time working with startups to find out what was going on in financial services outside the big organisations – that she realised how banks needed to change. She joined Allied Irish Bank as chief operating officer and began implementing some of the ideas she’d had while working with small fintech groups. This was successful for the bank, but Boden wanted more – and realised the only way to get it was by starting from scratch with a new bank when the time was right.

raw_text:
The AI build-out will not cause a repeat of the 2008 financial crisis. It is far more likely to cause a repeat of 2000, and that is not the reassurance it sounds like. A dotcom-style bust would still wipe trillions from markets, take a decade or more to recover, and arrive at a moment when the world has less slack to absorb it than it had in either 2000 or 2008.

I watched The Big Short again this week. What struck me was not the collapse. It was the 18 months before it, when a handful of investors read the loan tapes, saw that the collateral could not support the paper, and bought insurance against it while the sellers kept selling.

Boards ask me a simple question. Could the AI bubble produce a crisis on the scale of the subprime collapse, one that freezes credit, takes down counterparties and reaches every balance sheet on the planet? My answer has three parts. A sharp correction is now more likely than not within two to three years. The shape of that correction will look more like the dot-com bust than Lehman. And a full 2008-scale systemic event is a minority outcome, perhaps one chance in five. One in five is not a tail risk. It is a planning assumption.

The reasons the systemic probability is lower than 2008 are structural. So are the reasons the correction probability is high. Both deserve a plain explanation, because the damage will not land where most executives think it will.

2008 vs. 2000

Subprime was not a housing problem. It was a leverage and disclosure problem that used housing as raw material. Mortgages became bonds, bonds became collateralised debt obligations (CDOs), which became synthetic CDOs referencing other CDOs. The paper outstanding was a multiple of the loans beneath it, and the demand for it was partly manufactured. Goldman Sachs sold more than $40bn of mortgage securities in 2006 and 2007 while its own desk, on the chief financial officer’s instruction, shorted the market. It did not tell the buyers – pension funds, insurers, unions and foreign banks.

Three features made it systemic. The banks that ran the payment system were the holders, levered 30 to one. The instruments were opaque, so nobody could price a counterparty. And the collateral was a single asset class that fell everywhere at once. Remove any one of those and 2008 becomes a bad year rather than a near-death experience for the global financial system.

However, the dotcom bust was a valuation collapse, not a credit collapse, and that distinction is the whole argument. The Nasdaq peaked at 5,048 on 10 March 2000 and fell 78 per cent to 1,114 by October 2002, erasing roughly five trillion dollars of market value. It did not regain its high until April 2015.

The companies that died deserved to. Only about 14% of Nasdaq-100 IPOs were profitable at the top. Pets.com booked $5.8m of revenue against a $61.8m loss and was delisted within a year. Cisco, the picks-and-shovels supplier to the internet, traded at 201 times earnings and 20 times sales.

Yet the banks held. The payment system never froze. The US economy had a short, shallow recession, and the technology turned out to be everything its promoters claimed. The losses fell on equity holders, on employees paid in options, and on the pension funds that had drifted into growth stocks. That is a very different casualty list from 2008, and it is why most investors today reach for 2000 as the comforting precedent.

The AI build-out by the numbers

AI stopped being an equity story in 2025 and became a debt story. American AI companies raised $217bn of debt last year, had passed $445bn by mid-August 2026, and are expected by Morgan Stanley to reach close to $600bn for the year. Hyperscaler leverage doubled from 0.9 to 1.8 times in roughly six months.

The cash that used to pay for this has turned. Google’s free cash flow went negative in the second quarter of 2026 for the first time since its listing. The paper that does not appear on any balance sheet has grown: Goldman counts $1.5tn of lease commitments, a trillion of which have not started, and another $1.5tn of purchase commitments for chips and power.

The second tier is where 2000 and 2008 meet. Neocloud providers such as CoreWeave carry debt approaching $50bn, mostly floating-rate private credit from Blackstone, Apollo, BlackRock and Magnetar. The collateral is GPUs with a three-to-five-year life. CoreWeave’s five-year credit default swap touched 1,195 basis points on 15 October, pricing a default probability above sixty per cent.

And the revenue to carry all of it is not there yet. Bain estimates the industry needs $2tn of annual revenue by 2030 to pay for its compute and will fall about $800bn short. MIT research found 95% of enterprises getting no measurable return on generative AI. OpenAI, valued at $852bn, does not expect a profit before 2030. This is the Pets.com problem at hyperscale: the spending is real, the demand is assumed.

Which crash is the better model

On the evidence, 2000 fits better than 2008, and the fit is uncomfortably close. Valuation is back at the 1999 level: the Shiller CAPE stands at 41 against a dotcom peak of 44 and a long-run median of 17. Concentration is worse than 1999: the top five companies are 30% of the S&P 500 against 17% at the dotcom peak, and the Magnificent Seven are a third of the index. Investor sentiment has already turned: 54% of fund managers surveyed by Bank of America call AI stocks a bubble and name AI the top tail risk. The single-day lesson has been given once, when DeepSeek’s cheap model wiped $589bn dollars from Nvidia on 27 January 2025. And the revenue gap, Bain’s $800bn, is the same gap that killed the dotcoms: infrastructure built for demand that had not arrived.

The differences from 2000 cut both ways. Nvidia trades at roughly 30 times earnings with a 53% net margin, not Cisco’s 201 times. The hyperscalers are profitable incumbents, not two-year-old IPOs. That is the case for a softer landing. But in 2000 the infrastructure was financed by equity that could simply evaporate. This time it is financed by half a trillion dollars of debt.

That is where 2008 re-enters. The analogy with subprime holds on opacity, manufactured demand and who ends up holding the paper. Hyperscalers guarantee the leases of smaller partners, creating contingent liabilities that surface only when called. The ecosystem is, in Robin Wigglesworth’s words, incestuous: the chip vendor invests in the model company, which signs a compute contract with the neocloud, which borrows against that contract to buy the vendor’s chips. It is the 2006 CDO daisy chain with better branding. And the holders are familiar: pension funds and life insurers anchor the bonds.

The analogy with 2008 breaks on the two things that made it systemic. The originators have cash: Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon can write down a trillion dollars of datacentres and still make payroll. And the regulated banks are mostly originating to distribute, not holding.

So the honest model is a hybrid. The hyperscalers get the dotcom outcome: a long, grinding equity drawdown that the companies survive and their shareholders do not enjoy. The neoclouds and their lenders get the Hynix outcome: debt converted to equity, shareholders wiped, assets sold at a fraction of cost. The private credit funds, insurers and retail vehicles in between get the 2008 outcome in miniature, without a taxpayer behind them. A decade-long hangover is the base case.

The cyber short

When the correction arrives, the thing that gets shorted is not a stock. It is the operational resilience of every business that has quietly re-platformed onto these providers.

Your security tooling, your identity provider, your fraud models and your customer-facing assistants increasingly run on inference bought from a neocloud, which bought the GPUs with floating-rate private credit, secured on a contract with a model company that is itself years from profit. In 2008 the question was whether your bank would open on Monday. In this cycle the question is whether the provider holding your data and running your controls is in receivership by Friday, and what the administrator does with the hardware.

Three consequences follow. Distressed providers cut security first, because security is a cost centre and the lender wants cash. Distressed providers get acquired fast, and hostile actors treat a rushed integration as an open door. And distressed providers sell compute cheap. When the 1873 railway bust ended, the tracks were still there and freight became cheap for everyone. When the datacentres are repossessed, inference becomes cheap for everyone, including the people running credential stuffing, deepfake fraud and automated vulnerability discovery against your estate. The attacker’s cost curve falls at exactly the moment your budget does.

  • FinOps practitioners are stepping up to manage AI expenses, optimise token usage and align cost-saving measures with sustainability goals to improve returns from AI investments.
  • AI-powered digital health tools are flooding the market, but providers must look beyond marketing hype and evaluate their vendors to select the right tools for their needs.

The verdict

A 2008-scale crisis needs a single collapsing asset class, leverage inside the institutions that run the plumbing, and paper nobody can price. The AI build-out has the first and the third. It has only partly got the second, because the banks have pushed the risk to private credit, insurers and pensions. A 2000-scale crisis needs stretched valuations, extreme concentration, infrastructure built ahead of revenue and a central bank tightening into it. The AI build-out has all four. My estimate: a correction that impairs a trillion dollars or more of infrastructure and takes the leading indices down by a third to a half is more likely than not by 2029. A Lehman-scale systemic event is roughly one chance in five. Neither number is a reason to relax. The dotcom recovery took 15 years in a far more forgiving world.

The investors who profited in 2008 did one thing differently. They read the collateral before the market did. For a board, the collateral is your supplier chain. The one thing that can be done right now is to commission a financed-supplier concentration review of every AI and cloud provider in your critical path before the next budget cycle, mapped to ISO 27001 supplier and continuity controls, with a costed answer to two questions: what happens if the provider fails, and what happens if the price triples.

Ian Thornton-Trump is fractional CISO at Inversion6.

title: Threat actor use of AI becoming routine, warns Google
raw_text:
Threat actor use of AI in malicious cyber campaigns is evolving at pace, with several trends emerging over the past three months that point to a fast-approaching inflection point, according to research published this week by the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant.

Google’s team said that while previously it had only observed “nascent adversary interest” in agentic capabilities, since the summer multiple threat actors have started to abuse open source, agentic pen-testing frameworks to automate elements of their intrusions.

“Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly,” the team wrote in its report.

“While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge.”

Some of the more popular open source frameworks being turned to malicious ends include Artex – recently the subject of an FBI advisory – Cairn, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, said Google. It said it had seen Cairn used in several attacks against targets in the aerospace sector in the US, while PentAGI has been spotted being used for recon and vulnerability scanning in cyber attacks against Asian organisations over the past couple of months.

Google said that both financially motivated cyber criminal gangs and nation state-backed threat actors were likely using these frameworks, and said that their further use was a virtual certainty. Moreover, said the team, “As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity.”

At the same time, threat actors are also using multi-agent systems and LLM-driven pipeline to automate the more labour-intensive parts of vulnerability analysis, including tearing down patches and weaponising proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. This is a grave concern because, in doing so, they can cut the window between supplier patch disclosure and in-the-wild exploitation.

The Google team suspects threat actors have realised it is more efficient to use LLMs to weaponise patched n-day flaws instead of uncovering new zero-days because they can zoom in on a finite set of source materials, compare differing source code versions, and examine PoC code, release notes, security research and even media coverage. In contrast, zero-day hunting requires them to cast a much wider net.

The team said this was evidenced in the fact that while disclosures and exploits are skyrocketing – as seen in Microsoft’s monthly Patch Tuesday updates – the number of zero-days has risen only marginally.

“LLMs are transforming how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited across public and enterprise infrastructure, shrinking the patch window for organisations. Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fuelled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don’t, creating additional verification work for defenders,” said Google.

Financially motivated threat actors are increasingly profiting from so-called LLMjacking – the theft of LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised environments and their subsequent resell through underground proxies. This activity ultimately enables malicious groups to overcome the sort of problems, such as access costs, token rate limits and geographic restrictions, that often dog legitimate LLM usage.

Google said such access was in high demand, and it had observed the underground cyber criminal marketplace moving to meet it – for example, by transitioning beyond the sale of mass generic identity dumps to placing a premium on verified frontier AI accounts and tokenised API quotas as turnkey utilities.

Mandiant said it had responded to several LLMjacking incidents in the past few weeks in which threat actors were racking up fraudulent charges exceeding $100,000 a day, and as high as $1m in some instances.

Information operations

Meanwhile, threat actors engaged in information operations (IO) – which can include state-sponsored espionage groups, inauthentic political monetisation (IPM) groups, and commercial organisations conducting influence-as-a-service (IaaS) operations such as private intelligence contractors and even unethical marketing and PR agencies – are leaning into full operational LLM integration, said Google.

Such groups routinely use LLMs now to produce synthetic media, clickbait and other forms of AI slop, as well as harnessing them to automate domain network workflows, for example SEO manipulation, editing and formatting of seeded articles, and automated generation and publishing of malicious information.

In August, Google said it observed an unnamed group using its Gemini API alongside tools from others to build an end-to-end IaaS platform to manipulate public opinion in Europe and the Middle East.

The platform was engineered to automate the entire IO lifecycle, from the creation of sockpuppet personas through media generation and distribution and automated posting on platforms. Analysis by the GTIG team found the threat actor’s prompts were focused on emulating organic grassroots engagement while evading detections and mitigations put in place by social media platforms.
